findings.label: Large last-dim cases are bound by per-element data-dependent atomic writes in the MTE3 (write) pipe
findings.backend_detail: Ascend 910B4, 20 AIV cores; msprof op_summary per-op pipeline ratios (aiv_mte3 = write-out pipe)
findings.inference: For every large case the write pipe is busy 97.5-97.6% of the kernel while the vector pipe is at 0.0% and MTE2 at 0.7%: the kernel spends essentially all of its time emitting the per-element `tl.atomic_add` of line 88 to data-dependent addresses, not computing or reading. The scalar ratio 0.132 (~2592 us at 2048^2, 651 us at 1024^2, i.e. ~0.62 ns/element of address work) is the only other activity. Because the destination side of the atomic is not affine, the write pipe services one exclusive read-modify-write per source element instead of a coalesced store.

findings.label: Atomic cost is per operation, not per byte: fp16, bf16 and fp32 all cost ~4.65 ns per scattered element
findings.backend_detail: Same shape and same 2048 programs in all three large cases; only dtype (2 B vs 4 B payload) differs

evidence.metric: implied cost per element (fp16 2048^2: 4194304 elements / 19499.325 us)
implied cost per element (fp16 1024^2: 1048576 elements / 4937.451 us)

findings.inference: A 2048^2 fp32 case moves twice the payload bytes of its fp16 counterpart yet costs the same 19.45-19.50 ms, and the 1024^2 case costs the same per element as both. The invariant is the number of data-dependent atomic operations (one per source element), so the bound is per-operation write-pipe serialization, not bytes. Any change that keeps n non-affine writes per row cannot improve these cases; only reducing the number of non-affine writes (deduplicating before the write) can.

findings.label: The output copy is negligible and already streaming-class, so bytes/HBM are not the constraint
findings.backend_detail: Logical effective throughput only; not a calibrated HBM roofline

evidence.metric: _copy_flat_kernel avg_duration_us (fp16 2048^2, 512 blocks, 16.8 MB in + 16.8 MB out)

findings.inference: The bulk copy moves ~33.6 MB in 20.1 us and is 0.10% of the 19.5 ms call, so neither the two-kernel structure nor the input/output byte volume explains the loss. Affine streamed writes are orders of magnitude cheaper per byte than a scattered atomic write; the gap is architectural to the non-affine destination, not bandwidth saturation.

findings.label: 128x128 cases are host/launch bound: the device kernel is only 17.9% of the measured call
findings.backend_detail: Kernel time is msprof diagnostic; the walltime ratio comes from the authoritative eval latency
findings.inference: The authoritative eval latency for this same workload is 0.100691 ms while the only device kernel is 17.94 us, so ~82.8 us (82%) of each call is host work: Python dispatch, torch.empty_like and the Triton wrapper launch. The dense kernel itself is already conflict-free (no atomic, vector 0.618, write pipe 0.027) and its 2.10M pair-compares plus 16K loads/stores fit in 17.94 us. Round 4's host trim cut the eval latency of timing-0/3/6 by 8.9% / 12.9% / 11.0%, which confirms this path is on the critical path and that host cost, not the kernel, bounds the small family.

findings.label: The existing quadratic conflict-free dense formulation does not scale to ncols >= 1024 (measured per-pair rate)
findings.backend_detail: Projection assumes per-pair cost is roughly constant in ncols; larger per-program work could reduce tile overhead somewhat

evidence.metric: measured dense-path pair rate: 128 programs x (128 dst x 128 src = 16384 pairs) = 2.10M pairs in 17.94 us
projected dense-path time at 1024^2 (1.074e9 pairs) vs measured atomic kernel time
projected dense-path time at 2048^2 (8.59e9 pairs) vs measured atomic kernel time

findings.inference: Scaling the measured 128^2 dense rate (117 pairs/ns, which already includes that kernel's per-program scalar overhead of 0.535 within 18.9 us) to the large shapes gives 9.2 ms and 73.4 ms, both worse than today's 4.94 ms and 19.50 ms. Raising the `n * ncols < 903*n + 1.077e7` threshold to admit 1024^2/2048^2 would therefore regress these cases, and the O(ncols^2) compare-and-reduce family only helps these shapes if the pair rate improves 2-4x. This is an arithmetic projection from one measured point, not a measurement of a large dense kernel, hence medium confidence.

performance_interpretation: Round-4 state: geo_mean 0.34714 (+5.13% over round 3's 0.33021), with 6 of 9 timing workloads at 0.172-0.174x and 3 at 1.387-1.445x. The frozen hypothesis (the 128^2 family is host/launch bound; host trimming lifts timing-0/3/6 by ~6-7% and leaves the 1024^2/2048^2 cases unchanged) is SUPPORTED: the 128^2 device kernel is 17.94 us inside a 100.69 us call, and the large cases moved by only -0.02% to +0.15% (timing-1 -0.02%, timing-2 +0.04%, timing-4 +0.15%, timing-5 +0.01%, timing-7 -0.07%, timing-8 -0.02%). The same evidence defines that hypothesis's ceiling: host work cannot move the large family, whose kernel is 97.5% write-pipe busy with per-element atomics at a dtype-independent 4.65 ns/element. Two regimes need different mechanisms: (a) 1024^2/2048^2 - eliminate data-dependent atomics, 6 of 9 workloads with ~2x geo_mean leverage; (b) 128^2 - reduce the remaining ~83 us of host launch overhead, 3 of 9 workloads with up to ~2.5x if the 17.94 us kernel becomes dominant again. The measured copy (20 us, 0.10% of the call) and the measured dense pair rate (117 pairs/ns, projecting to 9.2 and 73.4 ms) both argue against byte-level or quadratic-conflict-free fixes at 2048^2. No quantitative Roofline is claimed: no calibrated hardware bandwidth bound and no reference-side counters were collected this round, and simulator instruction collection was not attempted on these 4.9-19.5 ms kernels.

next_experiment.action_description: Remove the per-element data-dependent `tl.atomic_add` from `_scatter_add_lastdim_kernel` (line 88) for the large last-dim family (ncols >= 512: timing-1/2/4/5/7/8). Step 1, bounded probe (minutes, not a formal eval): compile a debug variant of the same kernel that issues a plain `tl.store` at exactly the same data-dependent addresses with the same grid (2048 programs, BLOCK = ncols) and run it once on scatter_add-timing-2 through a Debug Job, to measure the write pipe without the atomic read-modify-write. Step 2, the ship decision: if the plain-store variant is at least 3x faster than the 19.499 ms atomic kernel, implement the conflict-free write path behind one `ncols` threshold constant - per-row bitonic sort of (idx, value) in UB, segmented fp32 accumulation of equal-index runs, then one non-atomic store per unique destination, keeping the copy kernel; if the probe shows a plain scattered store also costs ~4.65 ns/element, do not ship a rewrite, keep the atomic kernel and record the negative result so this axis is not retried blindly.
next_experiment.expected_impact: The six large cases carry 6/9 of geo_mean at 0.172-0.174x while the reference sits near 0.80-0.85 ns/element, so removing the per-atomic cost has a real ceiling: a 2x improvement (timing-2 ~9.7 ms, speedup ~0.35) raises geo_mean from 0.347 to about 0.55, a 3x improvement to about 0.72. A rejected probe costs one short Debug Job and leaves the current 0.347 intact, which is why the probe gates the rewrite.
next_experiment.risks_and_rollback: Sort plus segmented reduce is a substantial change: duplicate index values must still be summed, fp32 accumulation and the output cast must keep rtol/atol 0.015 (fp16/bf16) and 1e-4 (fp32) at matched_ratio 1.0, the 2048-element per-row working set (int32 keys plus values) must fit the 192 KiB UB, and the new path must keep a profiler-compatible launch (standard launch fallback). Rollback is a single-line revert of the ncols threshold so the validated atomic kernel keeps serving those shapes; do not narrow the correctness workload set or change tolerances.
success_criteria: Step 1: a Debug Job on scatter_add-timing-2 reports the plain-store variant's kernel duration and write-pipe ratio with the same addresses/blocks as line 88, so the atomic-vs-store split is measured rather than assumed.
If shipped: one full KGS eval returns status PASSED with all 9 correctness workloads at matched_ratio 1.0 and unchanged tolerances.

If shipped: geo_mean must exceed the round-4 0.34714 and the per-case actual candidate latency must fall for the targeted cases (timing-1 from 4.9555 ms, timing-2 from 19.5486 ms, timing-5 from 19.5542 ms, timing-8 from 19.5196 ms); a slower reference in the same run is not counted as improvement.

If shipped: msprof on timing-2 must show the atomic kernel's aiv_mte3_ratio (0.976) drop and the vector/write split change, matching the predicted mechanism; latency moving without the expected counter change (or the reverse) falsifies the hypothesis and must be recorded.
If the probe rejects the rewrite: keep the current source unchanged and record the probe artifact so the 0.347 geo_mean and the passing contract are preserved.

warnings: Profiler timings are diagnostic; all speedups and latencies in this analysis come from the frozen round-4 eval snapshot.
Pipeline ratios are marginal per-pipe activity, not a time decomposition or peak utilization; vector 0.0% with write pipe 97.6% does not mean 97.6% of peak bandwidth was reached.
Reference-side device counters were not collected this round, so no quantitative Roofline or candidate-versus-reference counter comparison is asserted.
open_questions: Does a non-atomic data-dependent scattered `tl.store` cost materially less than the atomic read-modify-write on this device? This single unknown decides whether sort-and-store (or any dedup write scheme) can beat 19.5 ms, and it is not resolvable from the metrics collected this round.

The reference path reaches 3.36 ms at 2048^2 (~0.80 ns/element); its kernel mix suggests a cube-assisted conflict-free reduction, but no reference-side counter set was collected this round, so this is unverified and must not be assumed to be a pure DMA or pure vector path.

Whether a 2048-element per-row sort plus segmented accumulation can be expressed in FlagTree Triton 3.5.1 (tl.sort or explicit compare-exchange) without exceeding the 192 KiB UB or the compile budget is untested.

The residual ~82.8 us of host work on the 128^2 cases is not decomposed this round: Python dispatch, torch.empty_like and the Triton wrapper launch are candidates, and the parent's own probe measured the bare dense launch at 0.0655 ms, high enough to warrant its own measurement before another host-side change.

Simulator instruction collection was deliberately not requested: the smallest atomic-path case is 4.94 ms per call over 110 invocations, and the previous batch recorded simulator timeouts on cases of this size.
